---
title: '<span style = "font-size: 18pt!important;">Intergenerational mobility of immigrants in 15 destination countries</span>'
subtitle: '<a href = "https://www.nber.org/papers/w33558" target="_blank"><span style = "color:#18BC9C!important;">NBER Working Paper (2025)</span></a>, <i>with 37 co-authors, <b>R&R at American Economic Review</b></i><br><i>Coordination: <a href = "https://lboustan.scholar.princeton.edu/" target="_blank"><span style = "color:#18BC9C!important;">Leah Boustan</span></a> and <a href = "https://fjaellegaard.com/" target="_blank"><span style = "color:#18BC9C!important;">Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen</span></a></i>'
abstract: '<span style = "color:#6C757D;">We estimate intergenerational mobility of immigrants and their children in fifteen receiving countries. We document large income gaps for first-generation immigrants that diminish in the second generation. Around half of the second-generation gap can be explained by differences in parental income, with the remainder due to differential rates of absolute mobility. The daughters of immigrants enjoy higher absolute mobility than daughters of locals in most destinations, while immigrant sons primarily enjoy this advantage in countries with long histories of immigration. Cross-country differences in absolute mobility are not driven by parental country-of-origin, but instead by destination labor markets and immigration policy.</span>'
